Katyn. The massacre was the systematic execution of between 4,400 and 21,857 Polish military officers, intellectuals, and state officials by the Soviet secret police, the NKVD, in April and May 1940 in the Katyn Forest near Smolensk and other locations in the Soviet Union. The victims were prisoners of war captured by Soviet forces during the invasion of Poland in September 1939. They were shot in the back of the head, buried in mass graves, and concealed. The massacre remained officially denied by the Soviet Union for half a century. Its exposure by the Nazis in 1943 became a Cold War propaganda battleground, and Soviet acknowledgment did not come until 1990, months before the USSR's collapse.

When the Soviet Union invaded eastern Poland in September 1939, it captured approximately 250,000 Polish soldiers and officials as prisoners of war. The captives were held in Soviet camps, particularly Kozielsk, Starobielsk, and Ostashkov. Among them were military officers, engineers, doctors, lawyers, and political figures. Stalin's regime viewed the Polish elite as inherently anti-Communist and a threat to Soviet control, and the decision was made to eliminate them systematically.

Between April 3 and May 12, 1940, prisoners were removed from camps in groups, transported to Katyn Forest and other execution sites, and shot in the back of the head. An estimated 4,400 to 5,000 were killed at Katyn alone. Thousands more were executed at other locations—Kharkov, Tver, and elsewhere—bringing the probable total to over 20,000. Bodies were buried in mass graves and covered, and the NKVD attempted to erase evidence, though burial sites were eventually discovered.

In April 1943, Nazi forces advancing eastward discovered the Katyn mass graves. They publicized the find as Soviet atrocity, accusing Stalin of genocide. The Soviet Union denied responsibility, falsely claiming the Nazis had committed the massacre. During the Nuremberg Trials, the Allies suppressed the Katyn issue to maintain wartime solidarity with Stalin. Cold War hostility prevented investigation, and the massacre became a symbol of Soviet brutality for the Western alliance.

Soviet denial persisted until 1990, when Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev acknowledged the NKVD's responsibility under Stalin. Declassified Soviet archives confirmed Stalin's personal authorization for the killings via a decision by the Politburo in March 1940. Poland and other affected nations recognized Katyn as a war crime and crime against humanity, though no prosecutions were ever pursued since Stalin and the perpetrators had died.

Katyn was part of a broader Soviet policy of liquidating Polish political and military elites. Estimated total Polish deaths at Soviet hands during the war exceeded 1.5 million. Other Soviet massacres of prisoners followed similar patterns. Katyn exemplifies Stalin's use of mass murder as a tool of state policy and demonstrates the power of secrecy and denial in concealing atrocity. The Cold War's suppression of Katyn—wherein Western allies, despite evidence, avoided condemning Stalin to preserve anti-Nazi unity—illustrated how geopolitical interests can override moral accountability. For Poland and the Eastern European nations, Katyn became a foundational example of Soviet domination and a symbol of nationalist grievance that fueled the anti-Communist revolutions of 1989 to 1991.
